keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem,
rootMeaning: The Greek verb στηρίζω (stērízō) derives from the root ἵστημι (hístēmi), which means to stand or set up. This etymological connection highlights the fundamental idea of causing something to stand firm or be firmly established. Unlike the English glosses that focus on strengthening or establishing, the root sense conveys a deliberate action of fixing something in place so that it remains steadfast and immovable.
usageInScripture: Throughout the New Testament, the verb στηρίζω appears thirteen times and is commonly translated with terms such as 'stablish,' 'strengthen,' and 'establish.' This range of translations reflects its consistent use in contexts of confirming or strengthening a person’s faith, resolve, or position. The word can denote both literal and figurative fixing, whether it be setting something physically fast or spiritually confirming a believer’s standing.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, στηρίζω underscores the divine and human responsibility to establish and strengthen faith and character. Its root meaning of fixing firmly reminds believers that faith must be resolutely set and steadfast, not wavering or unstable. This word enriches our understanding of spiritual growth as not merely growth but as being firmly grounded and confirmed in Christ. Such steadfastness is essential in the Christian life, enabling believers to stand firm amid trials and to be established in the truth of the gospel.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 9:51, the phrase 'he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem' uses στηρίζω to convey Jesus’ resolute determination and fixed purpose. The word emphasizes that Jesus decisively and unwaveringly committed Himself to the path leading to Jerusalem, foreshadowing His obedience to the Father’s will. This highlights the strength and firmness of His resolve, encouraging believers to likewise set their hearts firmly on God’s calling.
